### What happened?

`kubectl auth can-i  impersonate groups` or `kubectl auth can-i  impersonate users` unexpectedly expands any available groups or user crds in the created SelfSubjectAccessReview 

https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubectl/kubectl-commands#auth
>  kubectl auth can-i VERB [TYPE | TYPE/NAME | NONRESOURCEURL]
> TYPE is a Kubernetes resource. Shortcuts and groups will be resolved.

### What did you expect to happen?

Document any available syntax for checking impersonation permission on core resources "groups", "users", ... without an api group

https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/user-impersonation/
> To impersonate a user, user identifier (UID), group or extra fields, the impersonating user must have the ability to perform the impersonate verb on the kind of attribute being impersonated ("user", "uid", "group", etc.). For clusters that enable the RBAC authorization plugin, the following ClusterRole encompasses the rules needed to set user and group impersonation headers:
> 
> ```yaml 
> apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
> kind: ClusterRole
> metadata:
> name: impersonator
> rules:
> - apiGroups: [""]
>   resources: ["users", "groups", "serviceaccounts"]
>   verbs: ["impersonate"]
> ```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Given CRDs with group or user resource in various api groups
```bash
kubectl api-resources | grep '^groups '
#> groups                                                         group.harbor.crossplane.io/v1alpha1                    false        Group
#> groups                                                         group.keycloak.crossplane.io/v1alpha1                  false        Group
#> groups                                                         group.keycloak.m.crossplane.io/v1alpha1                true         Group
#> groups                                                         groups.gitlab.crossplane.io/v1alpha1                   false        Group
#> groups                                                         groups.gitlab.m.crossplane.io/v1alpha1                 true         Group
#> groups                                                         networkconnectivity.gcp.m.upbound.io/v1beta1           true         Group
#> groups                                                         networkconnectivity.gcp.upbound.io/v1beta1             false        Group
#> groups                                                         user.keycloak.crossplane.io/v1alpha1                   false        Groups
#> groups                                                         user.keycloak.m.crossplane.io/v1alpha1                 true         Groups

kubectl api-resources | grep '^users '
#> users                                                          sql.gcp.m.upbound.io/v1beta1                           true         User
#> users                                                          sql.gcp.upbound.io/v1beta2                             false        User
#> users                                                          user.harbor.crossplane.io/v1alpha1                     false        User
#> users                                                          user.keycloak.crossplane.io/v1alpha1                   false        User
#> users                                                          user.keycloak.m.crossplane.io/v1alpha1                 true         User

When trying to test such permission with `kubectl auth can-i impersonate groups`, the `groups` argument is unexpectedly expanded with the first available crd with name `group`

kubectl auth can-i  impersonate groups
#> Warning: resource 'groups' is not namespace scoped in group 'group.harbor.crossplane.io'
#> yes

#>  I0727 14:18:09.852572  171514 type.go:252] "Request Body" body=<

items.body:
As part of implementing [Conditional Authorization](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5681), in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138801 we did a literal rename from 

```go
if wants, ok := plugin.(WantsAuthorizer); ok {
	wants.SetAuthorizer(i.authorizer)
}
```

to

```go
if wants, ok := plugin.(WantsUnconditionalAuthorizer); ok {
	wants.SetUnconditionalAuthorizer(i.authorizer)
}
```

using a fully mechanical rename, with `authorizer.UnconditionalAuthorizer` corresponding to the authorizer interface that existed in v1.36, and `authorizer.Authorizer` growing new capabilities in v1.37.

The intention was to add `admissioninitializer.WantsAuthorizer` in a subsequent PR as a clean diff to show new usage of new features. 

If commit https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/833f712b4259a5a18a4bd4aee078f422dd3ec776, admission plugins that provide `SetAuthorizer(authorizer.Authorizer)` in v1.36 would either:

a) get a compile error in v1.37 if they locked their implementation like `var _ admissioninitializer.WantsAuthorizer = fooPlugin{}`
b) fail silently at runtime during `ValidateInitialization() error` as `SetAuthorizer` wouldn't be called

...until the admission plugin performed the same rename.

This code was initially part of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137633 (and its prefactor https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140715), but given this larger feature PR will not be part of v1.37, I propose to break out the commit to a dedicated PR, which targets v1.37 as a bug fix, to not break existing clients that depended on `admissioninitializer.WantsAuthorizer`.

/sig auth
/kind cleanup
/assign

### Which jobs are flaking?

pull-kubernetes-integration

### Which tests are flaking?

TestExternalJWTSigningAndAuth/signing_key_supported



### Since when has it been flaking?

The race condition has existed since the test was introduced in commit `6fdacf04117` ("Add plugin and key-cache for ExternalJWTSigner integration").
It became more frequent after commit `841886df76f` (2025-07-07, "Convert externaljwt from gogo to protoc"), which changed gRPC serialization timing and widened the race window.


### Testgrid link

https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/directory/pull-kubernetes-integration/2079278264051830784

### Reason for failure (if possible)

`WaitForSupportedKeysFetch()` signals via `sync.Cond.Broadcast()` inside the mock signer's `FetchKeys` gRPC handler — before the apiserver has processed the response and updated its key cache. After `Reset()` generates a new RSA keypair, the test immediately proceeds to sign a token with the new private key, but the apiserver still has stale public keys in its cache. Signature verification fails with `rsa.VerifyPKCS1v15` → `ErrCryptoFailure` ("go-jose: error in cryptographic primitive"), surfaced as "invalid bearer token".

items.body:
### What happened?

Argo CD controller crashed when the caller lacks RBAC permission instead of erroring. https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/issues/28607

`kubectl auth reconcile` panics with a nil-pointer dereference when reconciling a
`RoleBinding` or `ClusterRoleBinding` if the underlying reconcile operation returns an
error (e.g. a `forbidden` response because the caller lacks RBAC permissions)

**Proposed fix**: add the same if err != nil { return err } guard after
retry.RetryOnConflict(...) in both the *rbacv1.RoleBinding and
*rbacv1.ClusterRoleBinding cases.


### What did you expect to happen?

`kubectl auth reconcile `should return the underlying error (e.g. the forbidden error)
and exit non-zero, exactly as it does for Role/ClusterRole, instead of panicking.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reconcile a RoleBinding as a user without permission to get/create it:

```
cat > rb.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: test-rb
  namespace: default
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: some-role
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: nobody
  namespace: default
EOF
```

kubectl auth reconcile -f rb.yaml --as=system:serviceaccount:default:nobody

Instead of a clean forbidden error, kubectl panics:

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x0 pc=...]

k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/auth.(*ReconcileOptions).RunReconcile.func1(...)
        .../pkg/cmd/auth/reconcile.go:274 +0x...
k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/resource.(*DecoratedVisitor).Visit...
k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/resource.ConcurrentVisitorList.Visit.func1()
golang.org/x/sync/errgroup.(*Group).Go.func1()
```

### Anything else we need to know?

introduced in v0.35.0 and still present on master.
v0.34.0 guards all four cases correctly; the retry.RetryOnConflict rewrite that
landed in v0.35.0 added the retry wrapper to the binding cases but omitted the
if err != nil { return err } check that the Role/ClusterRole cases retained.

Found using Argo CD impersonation feature

items.body:
### What happened?

When kubelet runs an HTTP liveness/readiness/startup probe, it logs probe parameters at verbosity `-v=4` — and the logged fields include the raw `HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders` values taken directly from the PodSpec:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go:160-173
case p.HTTPGet != nil:
    req, err := httpprobe.NewRequestForHTTPGetAction(p.HTTPGet, &container, status.PodIP, "probe")
    if err != nil {
        logger.V(4).Info("HTTP-Probe failed to create request", "error", err)
        return probe.Unknown, "", err
    }
    if loggerV4 := logger.V(4); logger.Enabled() {
        port := req.URL.Port()
        host := req.URL.Hostname()
        path := req.URL.Path
        scheme := req.URL.Scheme
        headers := p.HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders              // <-- raw PodSpec headers
        loggerV4.Info("HTTP-Probe", "scheme", scheme, "host", host, "port", port,
            "path", path, "timeout", timeout, "headers", headers, "probeType", probeType)  // <-- sink
    }
    return pb.http.Probe(req, timeout)
```

`headers := p.HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders` is the user-supplied header list with **no redaction**, emitted into the `"headers"` structured field.

### What did you expect to happen?

The kubelet prober should not log raw probe `httpHeaders`. The `"headers"` field should be dropped or redacted (e.g. log only header names, or omit the value) in the `HTTP-Probe` line at `prober.go:173` — matching how other secret-bearing probe fields are handled. As written, attacker/operator-supplied credential headers are emitted verbatim into verbose logs.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops a same-package Go test under `pkg/kubelet/prober`, sets `-v=4`, builds an HTTP liveness probe with `Authorization: Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token`, calls the real `(*prober).runProbe`, and the fake HTTP prober returns `Success` — proving the leak happens **before** the request executes and does not require probe failure. Cleans up after itself; no cluster needed.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
F="$ROOT/pkg/kubelet/prober/zz_poc_probe_header_leak_test.go"
SECRET="Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"
trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT
cat >"$F" <<'GOEOF'
package prober

import (
	"context"
	"flag"
	"net/http"
	"testing"
	"time"

	v1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/intstr"
	kubecontainer "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/container"
	"k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/probe"
	"k8s.io/klog/v2"
)

type pocSuccessHTTPProber struct{}

func (pocSuccessHTTPProber) Probe(_ *http.Request, _ time.Duration) (probe.Result, string, error) {
	return probe.Success, "ok", nil // probe SUCCEEDS — leak is pre-request, not failure-only
}

func TestPOCHTTPProbeHeaderLogLeak(t *testing.T) {
	if flag.CommandLine.Lookup("v") == nil {
		klog.InitFlags(nil)
	}
	if err := flag.Set("v", "4"); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}

	pb := &prober{http: pocSuccessHTTPProber{}}
	_, _, err := pb.runProbe(
		context.Background(),
		liveness,
		&v1.Probe{ProbeHandler: v1.ProbeHandler{HTTPGet: &v1.HTTPGetAction{
			Path: "/healthz",
			Port: intstr.FromInt32(8080),
			HTTPHeaders: []v1.HTTPHeader{
				{Name: "Authorization", Value: "Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"},
			},
		}}},
		&v1.Pod{},
		v1.PodStatus{PodIP: "127.0.0.1"},
		v1.Container{Name: "app"},
		kubecontainer.ContainerID{Type: "test", ID: "container"},
	)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	klog.Flush()
}
GOEOF
OUT="$( cd "$ROOT" && go test ./pkg/kubelet/prober -run TestPOCHTTPProbeHeaderLogLeak -count=1 -v 2>&1 )"
printf '%s\n' "$OUT" | grep 'HTTP-Probe' || true
if printf '%s\n' "$OUT" | grep -F "$SECRET"; then
  echo "VULNERABLE: kubelet HTTP probe Authorization header leaked into verbose logs"
else
  echo "NOT VULNERABLE: secret header not observed in logs" >&2; exit 1
fi
```

Expected: a `prober.go` `HTTP-Probe` log line containing the secret in the `headers` field, followed by the `VULNERABLE` confirmation:

```text
I0702 11:32:34.631974 2674209 prober.go:173] "HTTP-Probe" scheme="http" host="127.0.0.1" port="8080" path="/healthz" timeout="0s" headers=[{"name":"Authorization","value":"Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"}] probeType="Liveness"
VULNERABLE: kubelet HTTP probe Authorization header leaked into verbose logs
```

### Anything else we need to know?

- This is secret disclosure of probe-configured credentials to kubelet verbose logs. It is a duplicate of the same finding already recorded internally as `kubelet_prober_http_probe_header_log_leak`.
- It is **distinct** from the recorded `kubelet_http_probe_header_log_leak` (sink `pkg/probe/http/http.go:119`, failure-only). This report's sink is `pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go:173` (pre-request), so successful probes leak too. Both are already separately recorded in the knowledge base.
- Affects HTTP liveness/readiness/startup probes; requires kubelet `-v>=4`. `TCP`/`Exec`/`GRPC` probes do not carry `httpHeaders` at this sink.

```
OK, yeah, I think this points to a (minor) bug in the token audience restriction:

These test cases fail:
* forbid create of token when audience in pod --> csi --> driver --> tokenrequest with audience and ServiceAccountNodeAudienceRestriction is enabled, csidriver not found
* forbid create of token when audience in pod --> pvc --> pv --> csi --> driver --> tokenrequest with audience and ServiceAccountNodeAudienceRestriction is enabled, pvc not found

The authorizer ends up not being called in these cases, which means that the authorizer-based bypass won't work for these cases.

### What happened?

kubelet exposes its resolved `KubeletConfiguration` at the `/configz` endpoint. When kubelet is run with `--manifest-url` and `--manifest-url-header` carrying credentials (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values **are returned in cleartext** by `GET /configz`, with no masking.

The codebase already knows these values are secret: the internal type tags the field `datapolicy:"token"`:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go:107
StaticPodURLHeader map[string][]string `datapolicy:"token"`
```

…and the **logging** path masks it before printing (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:288-291`):

```go
config := kubeletServer.KubeletConfiguration.DeepCopy()
for k := range config.StaticPodURLHeader {
    config.StaticPodURLHeader[k] = []string{"<masked>"}
}
logger.V(5).Info("KubeletConfiguration", "configuration", klog.Format(config))
```

But the **`/configz`** path does not. `setConfigz` (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:558-569`) converts the *original, un-masked* internal config to the external `v1beta1.KubeletConfiguration` and registers it:

```go
func setConfigz(cz *configz.Config, kc *kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration) error {
    scheme, _, err := kubeletscheme.NewSchemeAndCodecs()
    ...
    versioned := &kubeletconfigv1beta1.KubeletConfiguration{}
    if err := scheme.Convert(kc, versioned, nil); err != nil { return err }   // raw headers flow through
    versioned.GetObjectKind().SetGroupVersionKind(...)
    return cz.Set(versioned)
}
```

`configz` then serializes registered objects with plain `json.Marshal` (`staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/configz/configz.go:129-145`), so the header values ship out verbatim. The v1beta1 field is a plain `map[string][]string` with no custom marshaler and no `datapolicy` tag, so nothing redacts it.

`/configz` is installed on kubelet's authenticated server (`pkg/kubelet/server/server.go:648`) and runs through the auth chain (`pkg/kubelet/server/auth.go:108-109`): with `KubeletFineGrainedAuthz` it maps to `nodes/configz`; otherwise it falls under `nodes/proxy`.

### What did you expect to happen?

`/configz` should mask `StaticPodURLHeader` exactly as the logging path does (`server.go:288-291`) — on a deep copy before registration via `setConfigz`/`initConfigz` (`server.go:558-579, 775-776`), or omit the field from external JSON. The existing `datapolicy:"token"` tag and the logging mask express the intent; `/configz` silently bypasses both. Redaction must not depend on operators avoiding sensitive headers, since the field is the documented place to put upstream auth.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops an in-package Go test that calls the real `setConfigz` + `configz.InstallHandler`, hits the handler with `GET /configz`, and asserts the secret header is in the JSON response. Cleans up after itself; no cluster or running kubelet needed.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
DIR="$ROOT/cmd/kubelet/app"
F="$DIR/zz_poc_configz_leak_test.go"
trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT
cat >"$F" <<'GOEOF'
package app

import (
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"k8s.io/component-base/configz"
	kubeletconfiginternal "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/apis/config"
)

func TestPOCConfigzLeaksHeader(t *testing.T) {
	const name = "poc-configz-leak"
	const secret = "Bearer POC_STATIC_POD_HEADER_TOKEN"
	cz, err := configz.New(name)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("register: %v", err)
	}
	t.Cleanup(func() { configz.Delete(name) })

	kc := &kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration{
		StaticPodURL:        "https://manifests.example.invalid/static-pods.yaml",
		StaticPodURLHeader:  map[string][]string{"Authorization": {secret}},
	}
	if err := setConfigz(cz, kc); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("setConfigz: %v", err)
	}

	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	configz.InstallHandler(mux)
	rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
	mux.ServeHTTP(rec, httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/configz", nil))
	if rec.Code != http.StatusOK {
		t.Fatalf("status=%d body=%s", rec.Code, rec.Body.String())
	}
	if !strings.Contains(rec.Body.String(), secret) {
		t.Fatalf("secret NOT in /configz body:\n%s", rec.Body.String())
	}
	t.Logf("VULNERABLE: /configz body contains %q", secret)
	t.Logf("body: %s", rec.Body.String())
}
GOEOF
go test ./cmd/kubelet/app -run TestPOCConfigzLeaksHeader -count=1 -v
```

Expected: test **passes**, and the `body:` line shows
`"staticPodURLHeader":{"Authorization":["Bearer POC_STATIC_POD_HEADER_TOKEN"]}` — the header value in cleartext. (Against a real node: `curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer <kubelet-token>" https://<node>:10250/configz | jq '.kubeletconfig.staticPodURLHeader'`.)

### Anything else we need to know?

- This is secret disclosure of upstream-manifest credentials via an authenticated kubelet endpoint. It is a credentials/config exposure issue — any caller already trusted to read `/configz` (ops, monitoring, support) gains the manifest-auth credentials, which they were not meant to receive.
- Affects kubelet configured with `--manifest-url` + `--manifest-url-header`. Nodes using only `--pod-manifest-path` (file source) are not affected.

items.title: api-server does not always refetch JWKS on unknown key ID

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
### What happened?

We're performing regular key rotation of our signing keys used to sign tokens issued by our OIDC provider. Unfortunately the api-server does not properly refetch new signing keys.

The openid specification states that:
> The signer can begin using a new key at its discretion and signals the change to the verifier using the kid value. The verifier knows to go back to the jwks_uri location to re-retrieve the keys when it sees an unfamiliar kid value.

Source: https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#RotateSigKeys

However, as written above the api-server does not comply with that. Currently the api-server is using the coreos/go-oidc v2 library which only reloads keys when the cache-control max-age is reached. 

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected api-server to comply with the openid spec and immediately refetch keys if an unknown kid is seen.

This behaviour has already been changed in v3 of coreos/go-oidc library with https://github.com/coreos/go-oidc/pull/259. Keys are immediately refreshed if an unknown key id is seen.

However, this change has the potential to DDOS the issuer when someone brings an invalid token or a token meant to be for another cluster if the api-server (or the coreos/go-oidc library) does not rate limit such requests (as far as I can tell go-oidc does not rate limit). So some additional work might be needed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I can try to put together a reproducer later but I don't think it is needed at this point.

### Anything else we need to know?

On #sig-auth slack channel I found [this](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0EN96KUY/p1667778735333849) old thread from 2022 describes a similar/related problem. I believe all recent Kubernetes versions are affected by this bug. This would be fixed by #134454

/kind cleanup

/area kubelet

## Background

The following feature gates are currently deprecated and default to false:

- AllowDNSOnlyNodeCSR
- AllowInsecureKubeletCertificateSigningRequests

They were introduced as compatibility switches for the old kubelet CSR behavior around v1.31:

- AllowDNSOnlyNodeCSR allows kubelet serving CSRs without Node IPs, using DNS names only.
- AllowInsecureKubeletCertificateSigningRequests disables stricter NodeRestriction validation for kubelet CSR signers.

Both gates are still present in the codebase and documentation, although the v1.31 change notes described them as temporary compatibility gates.

## Proposal

I would like to clean up these deprecated feature gates in phases:

1. Confirm whether these gates can be locked to their default value `false`.
2. Add `LockToDefault: true` if required by the feature gate lifecycle.
3. After the required compatibility window, remove:
   - the feature gate definitions
   - the kubelet CSR DNS-only compatibility branch
   - the NodeRestriction insecure CSR compatibility branch
   - related tests and documentation

items.body:
`TestLegacyServiceAccountTokenTracking` in `test/integration/serviceaccount/service_account_test.go` tries to tolerate the date changing while the test runs by capturing `dateBefore` and `dateAfter`, but the assertion currently requires the observed date to equal both values:

```go
if date != dateBefore || date != dateAfter {
    t.Fatalf("Secret was labeled with wrong date: %q", date)
}
```

The same pattern is used again for the ConfigMap check later in the test.

That condition only passes when `dateBefore == dateAfter == date`. If the test spans UTC midnight, `dateBefore != dateAfter`, so no valid value can satisfy the check and the test flakes even if the implementation is correct.

I think both checks should allow either boundary date instead:

```go
if date != dateBefore && date != dateAfter {
    ...
}
```

I traced this back to the original test added in commit `569cd70a52359a294a608fb256693445a89a9dab`, and it still exists after the later flake fix in commit `6784610bebedb33f22259042c728a798c1e04b03`, which changed the concurrency/warning-count part of the test but did not update these date assertions.

If this sounds right, I can put together a small PR that only fixes the two assertions.

items.title: client-go certificate manager hardcodes ECDSA P-256 key type with no way to configure it

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

items.body:
### What happened?

The `generateCSR()` function in `staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go` hardcodes the key type to ECDSA P-256:

```go
privateKey, err := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), cryptorand.Reader)
```

This means all kubelet client and server certificates generated via the certificate manager use ECDSA P-256, regardless of what key type the cluster CA uses. There is no configuration option to override this.

The kubelet client certificate on the first control plane node is initially generated by `kubeadm` using the same key type as the cluster CA (typically RSA 2048), but on subsequent rotations it switches to ECDSA P-256 because rotation goes through client-go's hardcoded path.

### What did you expect to happen?

The key type for CSR generation should be configurable via the `CertificateManager` `Config` struct, similar to how `GetUsages` is already a configurable function. For example:

```go
type Config struct {
    // ...existing fields...

    // GenerateKey allows overriding the default key generation (ECDSA P-256).
    // If nil, defaults to ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader).
    GenerateKey func() (crypto.Signer, error)
}
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy a Kubernetes cluster with an RSA CA (default `kubeadm init` behavior).
2. Inspect the kubelet client certificate on the first control plane node — it uses RSA (same as CA).
3. Wait for certificate rotation (or force it by shortening cert lifetime).
4. After rotation, inspect the new kubelet client certificate — it is now ECDSA P-256.
5. On worker nodes, kubelet client and server certificates are ECDSA P-256 from the start.

The hardcoded line is at:
[`staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go#L767`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go#L767)

### Anything else we need to know?

- Environments requiring RSA keys (compliance, HSM compatibility, consistency with CA) cannot use built-in certificate rotation without patching client-go.
- Some deployments require ECDSA P-384 as P-256 is not considered sufficient under their security policies. The hardcoded P-256 makes this impossible without forking client-go.
- The `GetUsages` callback already handles the key-type-dependent usage selection, so the infrastructure for key-type awareness exists — only the generation itself is not configurable.

items.title: KMSv2: Write DEK expiration is indefinitely extended despite unhealthy KMS plugin status  (StatusResponse.Healthz != "ok")

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

items.body:
### What happened?

### Tl;DR

When a KMS key is disabled/pending deletion, the apiserver's write DEK ([kmsv2PluginWriteDEKSourceMaxTTL](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf56a97d5ec9747371ff221e8d320e819950083/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L93) = 3 minutes) is never allowed to expire. Writes continue indefinitely using the cached DEK, defeating the safety mechanism designed to stop writes when the KMS is unhealthy.

### Root cause

This happens because [rotateDEKOnKeyIDChange()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf56a97d5ec9747371ff221e8d320e819950083/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L405)  extends `State.ExpirationTimestamp` before the [Healthz != "ok"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf56a97d5ec9747371ff221e8d320e819950083/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L488-L489)  error is aggregated and returned. The function only checks if the `keyID` is structurally valid and matches the current state,  it does not check whether the plugin reported itself as healthy.




Basically, the state is stored with an extended expiration https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf56a97d5ec9747371ff221e8d320e819950083/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L406-L407  before `isKMSv2ProviderHealthyAndMaybeRotateDEK`  returns an error https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf56a97d5ec9747371ff221e8d320e819950083/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L488-L513 . Since the background health loop retries every 10 seconds [kmsv2PluginHealthzNegativeInterval](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d2c12afa4593e50a187075157d38748292b02733/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L92) on failure, and each retry extends the expiration by 3 minutes, the write DEK never expires.


#### Contributing factor (KMS plugin implementations)

Observed both major KMS plugin implementations return a valid `KeyId` in the StatusResponse even when reporting unhealthy status: AWS encryption provider [plugin_v2.go](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-encryption-provider/blob/6e294b39447208eba7895ae33c54a0d706ac3ede/pkg/plugin/plugin_v2.go#L131-L140) and GCP Cloud KMS plugin [plugin.go](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/k8s-cloudkms-plugin/blob/fea8970a7febc9565b195a6f617d018687b73662/plugin/v2/plugin.go#L97)

Also, Apiserver should not depend on plugin implementations to omit `KeyId` during failures in order to enforce its own write safety guarantees. The `kmsv2PluginWriteDEKSourceMaxTTL` mechanism is an apiserver-level invariant , it should be enforced entirely within the apiserver by gating [rotateDEKOnKeyIDChange()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c180d6762d7ac5059d9b50457cafb0d7f4cf74a9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L388-L414) on `response.Healthz == "ok"`, rather than relying on external plugin behavior to not return a structurally valid KeyId during error conditions. 



### Impact

**Security:** 

Data continues to be encrypted with a DEK whose backing CMK has been disabled/deleted. Operators expect that disabling a CMK will stop writes within minutes,  this doesn't happen.


**Operational divergence across instances creates confused experience to customer:** 

In a multi-apiserver setup, each instance generates its own independent DEK via [GenerateTransformer()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c180d6762d7ac5059d9b50457cafb0d7f4cf74a9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/kmsv2/envelope.go#L367-L418). Each instance can only decrypt objects encrypted by another instance if that other instance's DEK is present in its local read cache (an in-memory [simpleCache](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c180d6762d7ac5059d9b50457cafb0d7f4cf74a9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/kmsv2/cache.go#L37-L46) with a [24-hour TTL](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c180d6762d7ac5059d9b50457cafb0d7f4cf74a9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/kmsv2/envelope.go#L101)).

Since writes continue indefinitely (due to bug  above), every write calls [t.cache.set(state.CacheKey, state.Transformer)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c180d6762d7ac5059d9b50457cafb0d7f4cf74a9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/kmsv2/envelope.go#L281), which triggers [GC on the cache](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c180d6762d7ac5059d9b50457cafb0d7f4cf74a9/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/cache/expiring.go#L111). This evicts any other instance's DEK entries once their 24h TTL expires (measured from when that DEK was last Set() into the cache , via a prior successful [KMS Decrypt()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c180d6762d7ac5059d9b50457cafb0d7f4cf74a9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/kmsv2/envelope.go#L219-L231) call, not from when the CMK was disabled).

If the other instance's DEK was never cached (e.g., the [watch cache](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c180d6762d7ac5059d9b50457cafb0d7f4cf74a9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/delegator.go#L249-L262) always served the decoded object, bypassing TransformFromStorage entirely), reads fail on the first watch cache miss( example for K8s resource events), which could be minutes or hours after CMK is disabled.

After eviction or on first cache miss, reading an object encrypted by the other instance results in a cache miss → [KMS Decrypt()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c180d6762d7ac5059d9b50457cafb0d7f4cf74a9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/kmsv2/envelope.go#L219-L227) call → fails because the CMK is disabled → 500 error.

As a consequence, each instance can still write and read its own objects indefinitely (its own DEK is refreshed in cache on every write, as long instance doesn't restart), but fails to read objects written by the other instance. This produces 500s that depend on which apiserver the request lands on and which instance last wrote the object in question.

### What did you expect to happen?

When kmsv2PluginWriteDEKSourceMaxTTL (3 minutes) expires and the KMS plugin reports unhealthy status, writes should fail with an error indicating the DEK has expired. This is the stated design intent per the comments https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d2c12afa4593e50a187075157d38748292b02733/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L394-L397


Two fold fixes:

-  Gate rotateDEKOnKeyIDChange on health status in APIServer
-  Document KMSv2 plugin contract that plugins SHOULD return an `empty KeyId` when `Healthz != "ok"`, so that `ValidateKeyID`  fails https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf56a97d5ec9747371ff221e8d320e819950083/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L503 and `rotateDEKOnKeyIDChange` is never called. Then fix `aws-encryption` and `google-cloud-kms` plugins to return `empty KeyID`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. create a secret
2. update the secret
3. disable the key 
5. update the secret  ( this operations succeeds 3mins after disabling key)

items.body:
### What happened?

After upgrading a Talos Kubernetes cluster from v1.35 to v1.36, some running pods stopped receiving projected service account token rotations. The affected pods were not terminating.

During the control-plane restart window, kubelet logged transient TokenRequest / NodeAuthorizer failures like:

`Error preparing data for projected volume sa-token for pod network/external-5f8b6fdd5c-g4vzm: failed to fetch token: serviceaccounts "external" is forbidden: User "system:node:k8s-1" cannot create resource "serviceaccounts/token" in API group "" in the namespace "network": no relationship found between node 'k8s-1' and this object`

There were also kubelet TokenRequest EOFs against the local API endpoint:

`Couldn't update token: Post "https://127.0.0.1:7445/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/serviceaccounts/default/token": EOF`

After the API server became healthy again, the projected token files stayed stale for hours. Example affected pod:

pod: network/external-5f8b6fdd5c-g4vzm
node: k8s-1
token iat: 2026-04-28T20:46:41Z
token exp: 2026-04-28T21:46:41Z
projected volume symlink stayed at: ..2026_04_28_20_46_41...

A second pod on another node had a token issued at 2026-04-28T20:52:02Z, expiring at 2026-04-28T21:52:02Z, and also remained frozen at that timestamp.

The application impact was Envoy Gateway data-plane pods failing xDS authentication after token expiry:

`failed to validate token {"error": "token review found error: [invalid bearer token, service account token has expired]"}`

Because the Envoy data-plane could not reconnect to xDS, it kept stale endpoint config until the pods were restarted.


### What did you expect to happen?

For running pods, kubelet should keep retrying projected service account token refresh after transient TokenRequest/API server/NodeAuthorizer failures.

A temporary failure during apiserver restart should not leave the projected token file permanently stale or expired. Once the apiserver/NodeAuthorizer state is healthy again, kubelet should recover token rotation without
requiring the pod to be restarted.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I do not yet have a minimal deterministic reproducer, but the observed incident was:

1. Run a pod with a projected service account token, for example expirationSeconds: 3600.
2. Restart or upgrade the control plane while kubelet is refreshing projected tokens.
3. During the restart, kubelet receives TokenRequest failures such as:
   serviceaccounts "<name>" is forbidden ... no relationship found between node '<node>' and this object
   or EOFs from the API endpoint.
4. Wait past the projected token expiration.
5. Inspect the projected token file/symlink inside the pod or from the host.
6. Observe that the token remains expired and the projected volume timestamp does not advance, even after the API server is healthy again.
7. Restarting the pod causes a fresh token to be mounted and resolves the issue.


### Anything else we need to know?

This does not appear to be an application-level token caching issue. In the observed case, Envoy’s SDS secret last-updated timestamp matched the projected token file timestamp. The file itself stopped changing.

This also seems different from:

- #116481, which involves terminating pods/preStop hooks.
- #130442, which involved PVCs in terminating state.

The affected pods here were ordinary running pods.

items.body:
## Summary

A source-code audit of the kube-apiserver RBAC, admission, and authentication subsystems found that the default `edit` ClusterRole grants the `impersonate` verb on `serviceaccounts`, enabling namespace-scoped privilege escalation when privileged ServiceAccounts exist in the same namespace.

This behavior is acknowledged in code comments (`bootstrappolicy/policy.go:157` labels it an "escalating resource") and KEP 5284 introduces constrained impersonation as a replacement, but the risk is not prominently documented in the ClusterRole reference pages and most cluster operators are unaware.

## Impact

Any user with `edit` (via RoleBinding) in namespace X can:
1. Impersonate **any** ServiceAccount in namespace X via `Impersonate-User: system:serviceaccount:X:<name>`
2. Inherit all permissions of that ServiceAccount, including ClusterRoleBindings
3. If any SA in the namespace has `admin` or `cluster-admin` privileges (common for CI/CD, GitOps, and monitoring SAs), this is a direct privilege escalation path

The `admin` ClusterRole also inherits this rule via aggregation.

## Reproduction

```bash
# User has "edit" RoleBinding in namespace "production"
# "deploy-bot" SA in the same namespace has admin ClusterRoleBinding

kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:production:deploy-bot
kubectl get secrets -n production --as=system:serviceaccount:production:deploy-bot
kubectl create rolebinding escalate --clusterrole=admin \
  --user=attacker -n production \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:production:deploy-bot
```

## Scope Limitations

- Namespace-scoped only (RoleBinding in X does not grant impersonation in Y)
- SA-only (edit does not grant impersonate on users, groups, UIDs, or extras)
- Impersonation chaining is blocked (headers stripped before forwarding)

## Requests

1. **Documentation:** Add a prominent security note to the `edit` and `admin` ClusterRole reference documentation warning that these roles include ServiceAccount impersonation
2. **Hardening guidance:** Recommend operators audit SA bindings in namespaces where `edit`/`admin` is granted
3. **Consider removing `impersonate` from `editRules()`** in `bootstrappolicy/policy.go:159`, gated behind a feature flag if needed for backward compatibility
4. **Accelerate KEP 5284** constrained impersonation as the long-term replacement

## Code References

- Bootstrap policy rule: `plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/policy.go:159`
- Impersonation filter: `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/filters/impersonation/impersonation.go:74-118`
- "Escalating resource" comment: `bootstrappolicy/policy.go:157`
- KEP 5284: constrained impersonation (`staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/filters/impersonation/constrained_impersonation.go:41`)

## Full Audit Report

The complete audit (9 findings across RBAC, admission, and authn — 420 Go files reviewed) is published in the OSS Security Knowledge Base:

https://github.com/travis-burmaster/oss-security-kb/blob/main/wiki/kubernetes/kube-apiserver.md

## Additional Findings

The same audit identified three additional medium-severity issues in the admission control subsystem:
- Admission reinvocation skips newly-matching webhooks after label mutation
- Dry-run requests silently skip webhooks with `failurePolicy: Ignore` + `sideEffects: nil`
- Fail-open webhook bypass via induced timeout/network disruption

Details in the full audit report linked above.

# DRA Granular Status Authorization: Migration Guide

Starting in Kubernetes v1.36, the `DRAResourceClaimGranularStatusAuthorization` feature gate
(beta, on-by-default) enforces fine-grained authorization checks for `ResourceClaim` status
updates. Components that previously only needed `update`/`patch` on `resourceclaims/status`
now require additional permissions on **synthetic subresources** depending on which status
fields they modify.

Reference: #134947, https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/55070

---

## What changed

| Old permission | New additional permission required | Who needs it |
|---|---|---|
| `resourceclaims/status` `update`/`patch` | `resourceclaims/binding` `update`/`patch` | Schedulers, allocation controllers (anything modifying `status.allocation` or `status.reservedFor`) |
| `resourceclaims/status` `update`/`patch` | `resourceclaims/driver` `associated-node:update`/`associated-node:patch` | Node-local DRA drivers (ServiceAccount bound to a specific node via pod-bound token) |
| `resourceclaims/status` `update`/`patch` | `resourceclaims/driver` `arbitrary-node:update`/`arbitrary-node:patch` | Control-plane DRA drivers, network controllers, or any component managing device status across nodes |

The existing `resourceclaims/status` permission is **still required** — it remains the "front door".
The new synthetic subresources are **additional** checks on top of it.

These new permissions can be added **now** in preparation for 1.36, they are inert in earlier versions of Kubernetes.

---

## Migration by component type

### Node-local DRA drivers

These run as DaemonSets with a ServiceAccount whose token is bound to the node (via a pod
scheduled on that node). They update `status.devices` for their own driver.

**Add this rule to the driver's ClusterRole:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/driver"]
  verbs: ["associated-node:update", "associated-node:patch"]
  resourceNames: ["<your-driver-name>"]  # e.g. "dra.example.com"
```

**Keep the existing rule:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/status"]
  verbs: ["get", "update", "patch"]
```

### Control-plane DRA drivers / multi-node controllers

These run as Deployments (not node-bound). They update `status.devices` for their driver
from a central controller.

**Add this rule to the controller's ClusterRole:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/driver"]
  verbs: ["arbitrary-node:update", "arbitrary-node:patch"]
  resourceNames: ["<your-driver-name>"]  # e.g. "dra.example.com"
```

**Keep the existing rule:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/status"]
  verbs: ["get", "update", "patch"]
```

### Schedulers

These modify `status.allocation` and `status.reservedFor` when binding claims to nodes.

**Add this rule to the scheduler's ClusterRole:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/binding"]
  verbs: ["update", "patch"]
```

**Keep the existing rule:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/status"]
  verbs: ["get", "update", "patch"]
```

> Note: The built-in `system:kube-scheduler` ClusterRole is updated automatically
> by the bootstrap policy when the feature gate is enabled. Only custom schedulers
> need manual updates.

### Operators / virtual clusters that proxy all ResourceClaim operations

These need **all** of the above depending on what operations they proxy.

**Add both rules:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/binding"]
  verbs: ["update", "patch"]
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/driver"]
  verbs: ["associated-node:update", "associated-node:patch", "arbitrary-node:update", "arbitrary-node:patch"]
```

### Components that only read status or manage non-status fields

No changes needed. The new checks only apply to **writes** to `status.allocation`,
`status.reservedFor`, and `status.devices`.

---

An example of a simple wrapper around AuthenticationConfiguration:
```go
package v1

	metav1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"

	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/schema"

	scheme.AddKnownTypes(GroupVersion, &AuthConfigWrapper{}, &AuthConfigWrapperList{})
	metav1.AddToGroupVersion(scheme, GroupVersion)

	metav1.TypeMeta   `json:",inline"`
	metav1.ObjectMeta `json:"metadata,omitempty"`

	Config apiserverv1beta1.AuthenticationConfiguration `json:"config"`

// +kubebuilder:object:root=true

items.body:
### What happened?

I wanted to use a recently introduced feature called "image pull credential verification". It has been described at:

1. https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/images/#ensureimagepullcredentialverification
2. https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/2535-ensure-secret-pulled-images
3. https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/05/12/kubernetes-v1-33-ensure-secret-pulled-images-alpha/

I execute scenario with following conditions:

1. registry always requires authentication for the image in question
2. two sample pods are created which use the same image
3. pod definition requests to be scheduled to a specific node and it is always started there
4. the node does not have the image locally initially

The scenario:

1. pod A is started in namespace A without specifying service account or image secrets
2. default service account in ns A has a secret attached for the registry in question
3. kubelet pulls the image successfully
4. pod B is started in namespace B, the default service account has no secrets attached
5. pod B is successfully started but it should fail, this is the problem of this issue

This is what I observe. When the second pod is created an event is generated:

> $ k get events | grep 'already present' | tail -n1
> 42m         Normal    Pulled                 pod/sample-pod   Container image "zot.kube01.pemlab.net:5001/docker-io/rockylinux/rockylinux:10" already present on machine and can be accessed by the pod

This means the verification passed by it should not.

I have a standard configuration of kubelet with imagePullCredentialsVerificationPolicy set to NeverVerifyPreloadedImages. When this setting is changed to AlwaysVerify the attempt fails properly with message about missing credentials.

i did some digging in the source code to find the cause of it. On the second pod the kubelet thinks the image was not pulled by kubelet so it is treated like a preloaded image. After the first pod is created I see this:

```
$ jq . /var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled/sha256-dd81f502dc5e7f8b60445496abe590916d606411d7c474a2e18e4a42e4e82151
{
  "kind": "ImagePulledRecord",
  "apiVersion": "kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1",
  "lastUpdatedTime": "2026-02-14T09:41:58Z",
  "imageRef": "zot.kube01.pemlab.net:5001/docker-io/rockylinux/rockylinux@sha256:b86cb4305db4c29abb1e3a1257fefccc184b5e4a94378e02844b340845ef9460",
  "credentialMapping": {
    "zot.kube01.pemlab.net:5001/docker-io/rockylinux/rockylinux": {
      "kubernetesSecrets": [
        {
          "uid": "eeb25318-beff-46d0-bb24-f0c871a11e25",
          "namespace": "kube-system",
          "name": "zot",
          "credentialHash": "0bd56ac49132f1c4ffbf88affd024c6888e40d35fb6c9e10fef0e0b19a09fb06"
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

The ns A is the kube-system in this case. Note the imageRef as it will be used below. It has a proper sha for rockylinux:10 for linux/amd64 platform at the time this issue is created. zot registry is being used and the /docker-io/** path needs authentication.

The message is generated from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go#L257. The function receives argument of requestedImage with value "zot.kube01.pemlab.net:5001/docker-io/rockylinux/rockylinux:10". In imagePullPrecheck it uses imageService to resolve the image to an imageRef and it receives a value of "812a83d5aec123cbd962ba7cd1e22266db0fe2b3a0b49cb4e9aa521d13ad214f". It matches:
```
$ crictl inspecti zot.kube01.pemlab.net:5001/docker-io/rockylinux/rockylinux:10 | yq .status.id
812a83d5aec123cbd962ba7cd1e22266db0fe2b3a0b49cb4e9aa521d13ad214f
```

The call in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go#L253 uses the requestedImage and imageRef to decide if the image needs to be pulled or not. The MustAttemptImagePull contains a lot of conditionals and yet it doesn't have any debug logging. I had to modify the source code and add print statements everywhere to understand what is going on. The https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/kubelet/images/pullmanager/image_pull_manager.go#L211 tries to find by imageRef and returns nil, false, nil. There are no intents at this time so imagePulledByKubelet stays with false value. This in turn is processed by the policy and we have the decision.

Now I wondered why the find failed. The records are stored in memory. The lookup in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/kubelet/images/pullmanager/mem_pullrecords.go#L197 uses the imageRef into a map. The key isn't there. So I made an investigation when keys are added and the added key was: 

```
zot.kube01.pemlab.net:5001/docker-io/rockylinux/rockylinux@sha256:b86cb4305db4c29abb1e3a1257fefccc184b5e4a94378e02844b340845ef9460
```

and this is what is read from /var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled.

I tested this with cri-o and containerd. There is no difference. I wonder how this verification can ever work if there is always mismatch is inserted and lookedup keys ?

I have tested this with the directory clean and a fresh start of kubelet and the directory populated with files and the result is the same. The cache is populated with very long keys yet lookups are done with short imageID as reported by crictl.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect the kubelet to verify the credentials again but it doesn't do it.

items.body:
### What happened?

When the kubelet creates a `PodCertificateRequest` (KEP-4317, `certificates.k8s.io/v1alpha1`), it sets the owning Pod's `ownerReference.apiVersion` to `"core/v1"` instead of the correct `"v1"`. The Kubernetes garbage collector cannot resolve `"core/v1"` as a valid API group/version for Pods — Pods belong to the legacy core API group, which has no group prefix, so the correct `apiVersion` is simply `"v1"`.

This causes the GC controller in controller-manager to log errors like:

```
error syncing item" err="unable to get REST mapping for core/v1/Pod."
```

When a Pod is deleted, its associated `PodCertificateRequest` objects are never garbage collected.

### What did you expect to happen?

The `ownerReference` on `PodCertificateRequest` objects should use `apiVersion: "v1"` for Pod references, consistent with how all other core-group resources are referenced throughout Kubernetes. The garbage collector should be able to resolve the owner, and when a Pod is deleted, its `PodCertificateRequest` objects should be automatically cleaned up.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enable the `PodCertificateRequest` feature gate (KEP-4317) on the kubelet and kube-apiserver.
2. Deploy a Pod that triggers creation of a `PodCertificateRequest` (e.g., a Pod configured to use pod-identity certificates).
3. Inspect the resulting `PodCertificateRequest` object:
   ```bash
   kubectl get podcertificaterequest -o json | jq '.items[].metadata.ownerReferences'
   ```
4. Observe that `apiVersion` is set to `"core/v1"` instead of `"v1"`.
5. Delete the owning Pod.
6. Observe that the `PodCertificateRequest` is **not** garbage collected.
7. Check the kube-controller-manager logs for GC errors:
   ```
   error syncing item" err="unable to get REST mapping for core/v1/Pod."
   ```

### Anything else we need to know?

**Workaround:** A external signer controller can patch the owner reference from `"core/v1"` to `"v1"` on every `PodCertificateRequest` it reconciles. This restores proper garbage collection behavior.

First bug report, not sure if this should be opened here or commented on https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4317

I am happy to submit the patch for this myself, after I figure out the contrib process. :)

Affects all versions implementing KEP-4317 (`PodCertificateRequest` / `certificates.k8s.io/v1alpha1` / `certificates.k8s.io/v1beta1`).

items.body:
## What would you like to be added?

Add a `tlsServerName` field to the `TLSConfig` structure in `EgressSelectorConfiguration` to allow overriding the hostname used for TLS certificate verification, similar to the existing `tls-server-name` field in kubeconfig (added in[ #88769](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/88769)).

## Precedent

This functionality already exists in:
- **kubeconfig files**: The `tls-server-name` field was added in #88769 for similar use cases
- **kubectl**: The `--tls-server-name` flag provides command-line access
- **Go's `tls.Config`**: The underlying `ServerName` field supports this

The egress selector `TLSConfig` would benefit from the same capability for consistency.

## Why is this needed?

### Use Case

This addresses scenarios where components using EgressSelectorConfiguration connect through Kubernetes Service DNS names (e.g., proxy.svc.cluster.local) but that hostname is not included in the server certificate's Subject Alternative Names (SANs), which define which hostnames a certificate is valid for.

**Example scenario:**
- Egress selector is configured to connect to: `https://konnectivity-service.example.svc.cluster.local:8443`
- The proxy's TLS certificate contains SANs for: `proxy.example.com`
- Connection fails because `konnectivity-service.example.svc.cluster.local` is not in the certificate SANs

### Current Workaround Limitations

The current workaround of updating certificates to include all possible service DNS names has significant drawbacks:
- Requires certificate regeneration and rotation across many clusters
- Service names may vary across environments (dev, staging, prod)
- Certificate management becomes complex in multi-tenant environments
- May require coordination with external PKI infrastructure

### Proposed Solution

Add an optional `tlsServerName` field to override the hostname used for certificate verification:

```yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: EgressSelectorConfiguration
egressSelections:
- name: cluster
  connection:
    proxyProtocol: HTTPConnect
    transport:
      tcp:
        url: "https://proxy-service.example.svc.cluster.local:8443"
        tlsConfig:
          caBundle: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
          clientCert: /etc/kubernetes/pki/client.crt
          clientKey: /etc/kubernetes/pki/client.key
          tlsServerName: "proxy.example.com"  # <-- New field
```
This would allow connecting via the service DNS name while verifying the certificate against the actual hostname in the SANs.

### What happened?

Several years ago, there was an optimization made to the handling of WaitForCertificate so that it would be interrupted when the desired certificate changes, ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/77936. This optimization seems to have since regressed due to a race condition between when the `lastRequest` is retrieved by the `template` reconciler and when it's set by `rotate`.


If `lastRequest` is read by `template` before `rotate` sets it (and rotate is not actively trying to read from `templateChanged`), then the cancel function `template`  obtains from `getLastRequest` will be invalid as soon as `rotate` reaches the `setLastRequest` func. This means `template` essentially fails to cancel the wait in `rotate`, leading it to wait up to the full length of the timeout. Only after `rotate` independently exists the wait is `template` finally able to signal it at the beginning of the next iteration. 


### What did you expect to happen?

`WaitForCertificate` should break on the change of the certificate tmplate

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

One way to reproduce is just by creating a node, wait for kubelet to create the initial CSR, and then update the Node's addresses while the CSR is pending. In this case, a new CSR is not created until after the 15 minute timeout.

### Anything else we need to know?

Attempted fix in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131952, but this should be done as part of a larger refactor

items.body:
### What happened?

We recently developed a layer 7 load-balancing feature for kube-apiservers in our Gardener project.
While we tested it in a broad scope we discovered many watches which have been remotely closed by kube-apiserver. 
The root cause for this was `UnauthenticatedHTTP2DOSMitigation` feature gate. In our L7 setup which uses Istio/Envoy many clients could share one HTTP2 connection between Istio/Envoy and kube-apiserver. When the feature gate is activated each anonymous and each unauthorized request closes this connection and could kill the watch of several other clients.
This behavior is not desired since it creates lots of disruptions for various clients. In our case Istio/Envoy are responsible for mitigation of HTTP/2 "Rapid Reset" DoS Vulnerability. The connection between Istio/Envoy and kube-apiserver should not be affected.

This is also mentioned in PR #121120 which implemented `UnauthenticatedHTTP2DOSMitigation` feature gate

> Since this change has the potential to cause issues, the
UnauthenticatedHTTP2DOSMitigation feature gate can be disabled to
remove this protection (it is enabled by default). For example,
when the API server is fronted by an L7 load balancer that is set up
to mitigate http2 attacks, unauthenticated clients could force
disable connection reuse between the load balancer and the API
server (many incoming connections could share the same backend
connection). An API server that is on a private network may opt to
disable this protection to prevent performance regressions for
unauthenticated clients.

Deactivating `UnauthenticatedHTTP2DOSMitigation` is helping us and we are happy for now.

However, a feature gate is made to graduate in a future Kubernetes version. This would break our layer 7 load-balancing setup. We prefer to avoid this 😅 

### What did you expect to happen?

The mitigation of HTTP/2 "Rapid Reset" DoS Vulnerability should be a configuration option instead of a feature gate. This config option could be enabled by default.

This way, kube-apiservers deployed in a "standard" setup would still be protected while it would be also possible to deactivate it for a layer 7 load-balancing and an aggregated apiserver setup (see #122308).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Details about our issue can be found at https://github.com/gardener/gardener/pull/13405.

items.body:
### What happened?

Per APIServer track logs, there can be high latency (1s+) caused by `About to encode encrypted object` step in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f89e73a3038f06c98fedec7ece68bb101fc92638/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/kmsv2/envelope.go#L272-L282

The latency appears to come from `RecordKeyID` method due to lock contention: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f89e73a3038f06c98fedec7ece68bb101fc92638/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/metrics/metrics.go#L222-L229

There are a few issues in this method:
1. There’s a package level lock `lockRecordKeyID` that can cause a lock contention during high write throughput (a couple thousands writes per second).
2.  `Inc()` and `SetToCurrentTime()` doesn’t have to be called with `lockRecordKeyID` lock.
3. ~~Digging into `keyIDHashTotalMetricLabels` further, it appears that it only gets updated, but never used anywhere else.~~ It is used indirectly. Its eviction function is leveraged to delete labels from the metrics.

### What did you expect to happen?

The metric update should not be a bottleneck.
`Inc()` and `SetToCurrentTime()` don't need to be protected by the lock unnecessarily. Prom already provides thread safe guarantee for these methods.
~~KMSv2 has been GA'd for many releases. It's very likely that `keyIDHashTotalMetricLabels` cache is not useful and we can remove it.~~


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Throw high load (a couple thousands per second involving KMSv2) on the cluster.
Configuring KMSv2 to encrypt all resources can make it easier to achieve high write throughput.

### Anything else we need to know?

`RecordKeyIDFromStatus` in the same file has the same questionable pattern.

### Kubernetes version

Issue was observed on 1.33. But I believe other older versions can have the same bottleneck due to `RecordKeyID` has been there since 2023. 

### Cloud provider

It was initially observed on an EKS cluster. But this bottleneck exist in upstream.

items.body:
A security issue was discovered in [secrets-store-sync-controller](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/secrets-store-sync-controller) where an actor with access to the controller logs could observe service account tokens.  These tokens could then potentially be exchanged with external cloud providers to access secrets stored in cloud vault solutions.  Tokens are only logged when there is a specific error marshaling the `parameters` sent to the providers.

This issue has been rated MEDIUM [CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N) (6.5), and assigned CVE-2025-7445

### Am I vulnerable?

To check if tokens are being logged, examine the manager container log:

```bash
kubectl logs -l 'app.kubernetes.io/part-of=secrets-store-sync-controller' -c manager -f | grep --line-buffered "csi.storage.k8s.io/serviceAccount.tokens"
```

### Affected Versions

- secrets-store-sync-controller < v0.0.2

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

Upgrade to secrets-store-sync-controller v0.0.2+

### Fixed Versions

- secrets-store-sync-controller >= v0.0.2


### Detection

Examine cloud provider logs for unexpected token exchanges, as well as unexpected access to cloud vault secrets.

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact [security@kubernetes.io](https://groups.google.com/)

### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was reported by Reem Rotenberg and [Kas Dekel](https://github.com/privmickas) from Microsoft.

labels.name: sig/auth

items.body:
In order to avoid cache misses due to differently-ordered groups or extras, the `user.Info.Extra` attributes are sorted in the following code:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b8257c16678d1cd67db05a8224efe25192210c1b/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/authorizer/caching_authorizer.go#L123-L131

The extras are a `map[string][]string`. The order of the map keys is irrelevant here, and that is not what this issue is about. Rather, the above code changes the ordering of the string slice within the individual map values.

The caching was introduced in Kubernetes 1.27, with the following [rationale](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/f1700e4b95b404b37312084800ab8022f7069fee):
> This avoids the surprise of identical authorization checks within a policy evaluating to different decisions during the same admission
> pass, and reduces the overhead of repeatedly referencing the sameauthorization check.

This behavior is *de facto* the defined behavior, and has been so for seven releases. Therefore, this behavior should be documented by adding a comment to the code, and possibly also updating relevant documentation.

@liggitt has suggested making a pass through the code in order to determine if there was code relying on the ordering of the values within `user.Info.Extra` attributes (which we have now discovered has been unreliable since the implementation of caching years ago).

items.body:
### What happened?

Introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/4624cb9bb92186358e001be392e50e5d23b5cdd9, and only observable after enabling the `PodCertificateRequest` feature gate.

When https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2825 gets called, it queues PCRs for a given pod to be handled by a `podcertificate.Manager` instance.

However, if the queue keys for these PCRs get async-processed before https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2826 is called, the `podcertificate.Manager` will never again attempt to clear its internal state for these PCRs as kept in its `Manager.credStore` map.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet's state gets cleaned for a given pod when the pod is removed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Write a unit test that runs https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2822, expose the `podcertificate.Manager{}.credStore` variable, and observe what happens to the `credStore` variable when a cached PCR's state is supposed to get removed. Run a couple hundred times to make sure the race condition appears.

### Anything else we need to know?

Discussed at https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C05MW3382US/p1754992465556979

### What happened?

I am running the kubelet with a custom TLS certificate, using:

```yaml
tlsCertFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/kubelet.crt
tlsPrivateKeyFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/kubelet.key
```

I am automatically rotating this certificate using OpenBao. After some time, I see an error about an expired certificate:

```
> kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver-node-0 
Error from server: Get "https://172.29.0.2:10250/containerLogs/kube-system/kube-apiserver-node-0/kube-apiserver": tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid: current time 2025-07-16T19:47:40Z is after 2025-06-30T23:08:51Z
```

However, the certificate on disk is still valid:

```
# openssl x509 -noout -text < /etc/kubernetes/pki/kubelet.crt 
Certificate:
    Data:
        Version: 3 (0x2)
        Serial Number:
            7a:7a:b8:8e:ca:dc:61:19:f8:a7:07:ce:35:1a:ed:86:79:e8:21:bb

        Issuer: CN = Cerai kubelet CA
        Validity
            Not Before: Jul 13 19:54:43 2025 GMT

        Subject: CN = kubelet
```

It seems the kubelet is not reloading the changed certificate. Running `systemctl restart kubelet` fixes the issue temporarily (until the certificate expires again).

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect the kubelet to function correctly, as long as the certificate on disk is valid.

I haven't tested this reproducer yet, I will do that tomorrow. But I think the following should be sufficient:

1. Start the kubelet with `tlsCertFile`

items.body:
/kind feature
/kind cleanup
/sig auth

Previously since >= 1.29, we have promoted the feature gate `KMSv2KDF` to GA and currently the KDF enablement is locked to true via:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/05a596033cbe507053d6de79b8066c7f16076080/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L128-L130

With the KDF feature on, the cardinality of the cache for holding DEK seeds should be low and stable (unless the kube-apiserver keeps re-generating DEK seeds in pathological cases), so far most of the clusters we have seen have lower than 50 DEK seeds in the cache even though the cluster has been running for many years. 

Hence, we can consider replace the current expiring cache implementation with **non-expiring LRU cache** (e.g. with 1024 size) so that we don't need to rotate the cache on a day basis --- this helps improving the cluster's resilience to KMS service failures, say the KMS service is down for 5 minutes and if the cluster happens to rotate the cache during the time, it will result in unavailability drop unnecessarily.


Additionally, we can also consider pruning all the occurrences of `useSeed` checks from KMSv2 provider as it's no longer used.

items.body:
### What happened?

An incident was triggered by unexpectedly high etcd storage usage on production Kubernetes clusters. Initial analysis revealed that the majority of the space was consumed by a large number of Certificate Signing Requests (CSRs).

Using `etcdctl`, the top resource consumers in etcd were identified:

| Resource Type | Count |
|---------------|-------|
| **CertificateSigningRequests** | **520,858** |
| Events | 1,395 |
| CRDs (Calico) | 1,005 |
| ReplicaSets | 864 |
| RoleBindings | 473 |
| Services | 428 |
| Pods | 416 |

This overwhelming number of CSRs was far beyond what could be explained by normal node provisioning or rotation activity. A sample of 1,000 CSRs showed an average size of **1,192 bytes**, meaning the CSRs alone were consuming **~592 MiB** of etcd space—nearly a third of the 2 GiB etcd limit.

This dates on the resources showed the build up had been happening for years, with one being generated for each node every 15 minutes.

On examination they were all of the type:

```
apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1
kind: CertificateSigningRequest
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2025-07-09T06:51:01Z"
  generateName: csr-
  name: csr-jllx7
  resourceVersion: "296695671"
  uid: 0f6d31fd-c8ed-465e-ac45-e283f453f56c
spec:
  groups:
  - system:nodes
  - system:authenticated
  request: 
  signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet
  usages:
  - digital signature
  - client auth
  username: system:node:octavia
status:
  conditions:
  - lastTransitionTime: "2025-07-09T06:51:01Z"
    lastUpdateTime: "2025-07-09T06:51:01Z"
    message: Auto approving self kubelet client certificate after SubjectAccessReview.
    reason: AutoApproved
    status: "True"
    type: Approved
```

TLS Bootsrapping was disabled in our kubeadm config, and setting `rotateCertificates: false` had no effect.

Because we don't rely on the kubelet + controller-manager auto certificate handling mechanism for our nodes, the kubelets continued to issue client CSRs and the controller kept approving them.

We narrowed down the root cause to some cluster role bindings that were created automatically by kubeadm.

CRBs in question:
```
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: kubeadm:node-autoapprove-certificate-rotation
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: system:certificates.k8s.io:certificatesigningrequests:selfnodeclient
subjects:
- apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Group
  name: system:nodes 
```
and
```
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2023-10-09T23:54:31Z"
  name: kubeadm:node-autoapprove-bootstrap
  resourceVersion: "90650499"
  uid: 7d2c0095-b8c1-4b7d-baac-0f7b8edd0ec5
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: system:certificates.k8s.io:certificatesigningrequests:nodeclient
subjects:
- apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Group
  name: system:bootstrappers:kubeadm:default-node-token
```

Combined with [no logic in the CSR cleaner controller code accounting for the scenario of kubelet CSR's getting approved with certificates not issued](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.30/pkg/controller/certificates/cleaner/cleaner.go#L53-L61) means no GC and a build up over time of approved CSRs. 

Mitigation is to manually remove these cluster role bindings and to delete all old approved CSRs... all half million of them.

Is there is an alternative way to deal with the problem we're missing? If so the documentation could use an update.

Otherwise we propose the cleaner be updated with a condition to also remove **Approved** but not Issued CSRs in line with the documentation.
If there is a reason why we would not want to remove them in such a short period of time as the **Approved** GC timeline in the documentation, at least treating them the same as **Pending** i.e. 24hrs.


### What did you expect to happen?

- We expected these would get garbage collected in line with the GC policy where ["Approved requests: automatically deleted after 1 hour](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/certificate-signing-requests/#request-signing-process)" 
 
- if this condition is not included by design, documentation should be updated to explain it.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- kubeadm configured without TLS bootstrapping and with self managed certificate issuing
- Assert these [these cluster role bindings](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/kubelet-tls-bootstrapping/#approval) allowing the kube controller to auto approve the certificates.
  - `kubeadm:node-autoapprove-certificate-rotation`
  - `kubeadm:node-autoapprove-bootstrap`
- Wait 15 minutes and run check that kubelet CSRs that get created are now moving into an `Approved` state but never get issued certificates `kubectl get csr --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.status.conditions[]?.type=="Approved" and (.status.certificate|length==0)) | .metadata.name'`
- After exceeding 24 hours later they should still persist and be growing in count.

### Anything else we need to know?

HashiVault used for certificate signing. Not so much relevant but does gives context in our use case.
